summary: Defines the XML Configuration Access Protocol, which lets a client read, write and modify application configuration data stored in XML on a server. It maps document parts and attributes to HTTP URIs.

eli5.summary: A server keeps settings in a big XML file. XCAP gives every part its own web address, so a program can fetch or change just that one piece.

questions: how to edit xml with http uris
how does xcap map xml to http uris
what is the xcap node selector separator
what is an xcap application usage
subtitle: How plain HTTP can read and edit a single element or attribute inside an XML document on a server.

tldr.problem: Network servers for things like presence and instant messaging need per-user data that users manage themselves from many devices, and each application would otherwise need its own way to read and change it.
tldr.mechanism: XCAP stores the data as XML documents and gives every document, element and attribute its own HTTP URI, so that GET, PUT and DELETE can fetch, create, replace or remove exactly that piece, checked against rules defined per application.
tldr.outcome: Clients get fine-grained, conditional updates over ordinary HTTP, while each application defines its own schema, URIs and rules in a document called an application usage.

today: RFC 4825 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2007. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves the data formats to application usages such as the resource lists format in RFC 4826.

sections.title: The Problem XCAP Solves
sections.content:
In applications such as Voice over IP, instant messaging and presence, network servers need per-user information to handle requests. This data lives in the network but is managed by the user, who may reach it from the web, a wireless handset or a PC application. The RFC's examples are presence authorization policy, which says which watchers may subscribe to a presentity, and presence lists, which a Resource List Server needs in order to process a SIP SUBSCRIBE request.

The XML Configuration Access Protocol (XCAP) is a set of conventions for mapping XML documents and their parts onto HTTP URIs, plus rules for how changing one resource affects another, data validation constraints and authorization policies. Because of this, ordinary HTTP primitives can manipulate the data. It borrows ideas from the Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP) but does not extend it or depend on it.

The RFC also says what XCAP is not: it was not designed as a general purpose XML search protocol, an XML database update protocol, or a general purpose XML-based configuration protocol for network elements.
sections.eli5: People keep their settings on a server so they can use them from any device. XCAP is the polite way for each device to ask for or change those settings.

sections.title: How XCAP Works
sections.content:
Each application that uses XCAP defines an application usage. It names the XML schema for the application's data and several other key facts. An XCAP server is a repository of XML documents, with documents stored for each application and, within each application, for each user.

Every document, element or attribute is an XCAP resource: an HTTP resource that follows XCAP's naming and validation rules. Reading one uses HTTP GET, creating or modifying one uses PUT, and removing one uses DELETE. POST is not defined, because XCAP resources are not processing scripts. HTTP properties such as entity tags apply too, and are especially useful for conditional operations.

Two documents that look different can be equivalent, so the canonical form with comments of an XML document decides logical equivalence. A client should not expect a document it PUT to come back octet-for-octet identical, because of XML normalization and equivalency rules.
sections.eli5: The server is a filing cabinet of XML files. You use the web's usual verbs: get to look, put to write, delete to remove. Nothing fancy to learn.

sections.title: Application Usages
sections.content:
An application usage holds everything specific to one application. The RFC requires it to provide:

  • an Application Unique ID (AUID), registered with IANA for general use or prefixed with a reversed domain name such as com.example.foo for vendor use;
  • an XML schema, a default document namespace and a MIME type;
  • validation constraints, data semantics, naming conventions, resource interdependencies and authorization policies.

Schemas cannot express every rule, so the usage adds constraints such as uniqueness within a scope. Servers do not validate referential integrity, and clients MUST NOT depend on them for it. All XCAP documents MUST be UTF-8. The server is deliberately unaware of data semantics and only enforces schema validity and the usage's constraints.

By default each user can read, modify and delete everything below their home directory, and anyone can read the global documents, but only trusted, provisioned users can change them. A server MUST understand an application usage to serve requests for it, though it may accept content from namespaces it does not know, checking only that the XML is well-formed.

If a user needs just one document in an application usage, the RFC recommends calling it index and keeping it in the user's home directory.
sections.eli5: Each app has its own rule book that says what its settings file looks like and what is allowed. The server follows the rule book but does not need to understand what the settings mean.

sections.title: Building XCAP URIs
sections.content:
An XCAP URI is the XCAP root, then a document selector, then the node selector separator ~~, then a percent-encoded node selector, then an optional query that holds namespace bindings. The root is any HTTP URI without a query; the RFC recommends xcap.domain and gives http://xcap.example.com as an example.

The first segment of the document selector MUST be the AUID, and the next MUST be global or users. Under users comes the XCAP User Identifier (XUI), which for SIP systems is recommended to be the user's Address-of-Record, such as sip:joe@example.com. Subtrees below an XUI are called home directories. Subdirectories are allowed but NOT RECOMMENDED.

The node selector is based on XPath but far simpler. Each step must pick exactly one element, by name, by position, by attribute value, or by position and attribute. A wildcard may stand in for the name. The last step can instead pick an attribute (written with a leading @) or the namespace bindings in scope (the namespace selector). If a step matches nothing, or more than one element, the selector is invalid. Prefixes are defined in the query using xmlns() expressions. Comments, text and processing instructions cannot be selected, and whitespace is preserved exactly.
sections.eli5: The address works like a path to a room in a building: the building, the floor, the room, then the exact shelf inside it. The double tilde marks where the file name ends and the inside of the file begins.

sections.title: Client Operations and Server Behavior
sections.content:
Clients create or replace a document, element or attribute with PUT, fetch with GET and remove with DELETE. The content type matters: the usage's own type for documents, application/xcap-el+xml for elements, application/xcap-att+xml for attributes and application/xcap-ns+xml for namespace bindings. A namespace selector is read-only, so a PUT or DELETE to one is rejected with 405.

A PUT whose selector matches nothing is a creation, and one that matches something is a replacement. XCAP requires that after a PUT, a GET of the same URI returns what was PUT. Requests that would break this are rejected with a 409 and a cannot-insert report. Deletions are similarly restricted so that they stay idempotent. To insert at a position, a client uses a selector like parent/*[2][@id='new'], where the attribute predicate makes the selector a no-match so it creates instead of replacing.

The server checks, in order: whether it knows the application usage and the user (otherwise 404), authentication, authorization, then the namespace prefixes (an undefined prefix gets 400). It then validates the result against the schema, uniqueness rules and other constraints, and rejects failures with 409. A wrong content type gets 415. Success is 201 Created or 200 OK.
sections.eli5: To add a toy to a shelf you say exactly which shelf spot you mean. If the spot is already taken you would be replacing the toy, so you must name it in a way that shows it is a new one.

sections.title: Entity Tags, Caching and Conflict Reports
sections.content:
A server MUST keep entity tags for its resources, with one extra rule: all resources in a document share one etag. When any part changes, the whole document gets a new etag. Successful PUT, GET and DELETE responses carry it. A client can send If-Match with the etag it last saw and get a 412 if someone else changed the document, then re-fetch and retry. It can send If-None-Match on a GET and receive 304 if its cached copy is still valid. Because the etag is shared, a conditional PUT of an element or attribute with If-None-Match: * always fails.

Network caches do not know how XCAP resources depend on each other, so for data likely to be dynamic, servers SHOULD indicate a no-cache directive.

When a request fails with 409, the body usually holds an xcap-error document (type application/xcap-error+xml). Its error elements include not-well-formed, no-parent, schema-validation-error, uniqueness-failure (which may suggest alternative values), constraint-failure, cannot-insert and cannot-delete. A client SHOULD NOT simply retry a rejected request without changing something.
sections.eli5: The whole binder has one version sticker. If someone else changed a page, your sticker is out of date and the server tells you to look again before writing.

sections.title: Server Capabilities
sections.content:
Since XCAP can be extended with new application usages and protocol extensions, clients may need to know what a server supports. The RFC defines an application usage with the AUID xcap-caps, which all XCAP servers MUST support. It is a single well-known document in the global tree.

Its root element xcap-caps has three children: auids, extensions and namespaces. To list a namespace as supported, the server must have the schemas for all its elements and be able to validate them. The xcap-caps AUID itself and the urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xcap-caps namespace MUST be listed.
sections.eli5: There is a menu on the server that lists which kinds of settings it understands, so you can check before you try to write something it would not accept.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
XCAP data is often sensitive, so the RFC RECOMMENDS handing out an HTTPS URI as the XCAP root, giving TLS-encrypted traffic. Clients MUST implement TLS, and SHOULD attempt to upgrade connections to TLS.

Authorization of reads and writes needs client authentication. Servers MUST implement HTTP Digest, SHOULD challenge clients with it over TLS, and MUST NOT perform basic authentication without TLS. Clients MUST implement digest authentication.

XCAP runs on the same ports as HTTP, so port-based firewall rules cannot single it out. There is no foolproof way to tell an XCAP URL apart, though a double tilde is a strong hint that it points to an element or attribute, bearing in mind the many ways a URI can be encoded.
sections.eli5: Because the settings are private, you should send them in a locked envelope and show ID first.
